quiz.q: A patient four hours into chest pain has cold clammy skin, a systolic of 76, crackles to the mid-lung fields and distended neck veins. The correct management includes:
choices: A 1 liter fluid bolus wide open
Oxygen, keep him warm, position of comfort, and rapid transport to a cardiac center
Assisting with his nitroglycerin to reduce cardiac workload
Placing him flat with legs elevated
quiz.why: This is cardiogenic shock, where the pump has failed and only opening the artery helps. Fluids worsen pulmonary congestion, nitroglycerin is contraindicated at a systolic of 76, and laying a patient with crackles flat deepens the hypoxia.

quiz.q: Muffled heart sounds, distended neck veins and a blood pressure of 84/70 after a stab wound to the chest suggest:
choices: Hypovolemic shock from blood loss
Tension pneumothorax
Massive pulmonary embolism
Cardiac tamponade
quiz.why: Muffled sounds with jugular distention and a narrow pulse pressure of 84/70 is the classic tamponade triad. Hypovolemia gives flat neck veins, a tension pneumothorax removes breath sounds on one side, and a PE follows immobility rather than penetrating trauma.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old reports chest pain that began at maximum intensity and tears through to his back. His right arm reads 196/108 and his left reads 148/86. Your management should include:
choices: Aspirin 324 mg chewed and nitroglycerin 0.4 mg
Rapid fluid bolus and legs elevated
Withholding aspirin and nitroglycerin, contacting medical control, and rapid transport
Encouraging him to walk to the stretcher to assess exertional pain
quiz.why: Tearing pain to the back with a large inter-arm pressure difference suggests aortic dissection, where aspirin adds bleeding risk and nitroglycerin can be dangerous. Contact medical control, keep the patient still, and transport rapidly.

quiz.q: A blood pressure of 214/122 with a severe headache and blurred vision is best managed by an EMT with:
choices: Calm reassurance, head elevated, minimal stimulation and transport
Assisting the patient with his home antihypertensive
Lying the patient flat to improve cerebral perfusion
Withholding transport until the pressure falls below 180 systolic
quiz.why: This is a hypertensive emergency and EMTs do not lower blood pressure, because a rapid drop can cause a stroke. Calm, head elevated, minimal stimulation and steady transport are correct. Assisting with an antihypertensive is outside EMT scope.

quiz.q: Which episode of syncope warrants the highest suspicion of a dangerous cardiac cause?
choices: A teenager who fainted after standing in a hot gym, with warning nausea
A 20-year-old athlete who collapsed suddenly mid-sprint with no warning
An adult who fainted while having blood drawn
An adult who fainted after prolonged vomiting and diarrhea
quiz.why: Exertional syncope with no prodrome suggests a structural or rhythm abnormality and carries a real risk of sudden death. The other three have clear vasovagal or volume-depletion triggers with typical warning symptoms and benign patterns.

scenarios.title: Dispatched: 58-year-old male, chest pain
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched at 1420 to a hardware store for a 58-year-old man with chest pain. Dispatch says he sat down behind the register and asked an employee to call. You carry aspirin, a 12-lead monitor, oxygen and a blood pressure cuff. Transport time to the nearest hospital is 12 minutes. The nearest hospital with a cardiac catheterization lab is 21 minutes away.

steps.prompt:
He is sitting on a stool, pale, with sweat beading on his forehead in an air-conditioned store. He puts a closed fist against the center of his chest and says the pressure started about forty minutes ago while he was stocking shelves and has not let up. He feels sick to his stomach. He has high blood pressure and high cholesterol and takes nitroglycerin for chest pain, which is in his jacket pocket.

What do you do first?

choices.text: Have him stay seated and stop moving, put him on the monitor, and get a 12-lead within 10 minutes of contact
choices.feedback: Correct. Stop the exertion, because every bit of work raises myocardial oxygen demand, and get the tracing that decides where he goes and whether the cath lab is activated before you arrive.

choices.text: Have him walk out to the stretcher so you can save time on scene
choices.feedback: Never walk a chest pain patient. Walking increases the heart's oxygen demand exactly when supply is cut off, and patients have arrested doing it. Bring the stretcher to him.

choices.text: Apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min right away
choices.feedback: His SpO2 is 97% and he is not short of breath. Routine oxygen in a normoxic cardiac patient constricts coronary vessels and worsens outcomes. The threshold is below 94%, dyspnea, or shock.

choices.text: Give aspirin immediately, before anything else
choices.feedback: Aspirin is right and it is coming. Confirming no allergy and no active bleeding takes ten seconds, and getting the 12-lead started at the same time costs you nothing. Order here is a minor point; skipping the allergy check is not.

steps.prompt:
The 12-lead is acquired at six minutes after contact and transmitted. He has no allergies and no history of ulcers or bleeding, and he has not taken any aspirin today.

What dose do you give and how?

choices.text: 324 mg, as four 81 mg chewable tablets, chewed and then swallowed
choices.feedback: Correct. Four baby aspirin equal 324 mg, and chewing speeds absorption so platelet inhibition starts sooner. This is the single field intervention with the clearest survival benefit.

choices.text: 81 mg, one chewable tablet
choices.feedback: Too small an antiplatelet load for an acute event. The field dose is 324 mg. One 81 mg tablet is a daily preventive dose, not an acute one.

choices.text: 650 mg of regular aspirin swallowed with water
choices.feedback: Wrong dose and wrong route. More than 324 mg adds bleeding risk without benefit, and swallowing whole tablets delays absorption when minutes matter.

choices.text: No aspirin, because he takes nitroglycerin and might be on other cardiac medications
choices.feedback: Being on cardiac medications is not a contraindication. The reasons to withhold are a true allergy, active gastrointestinal bleeding, or an inability to protect the airway.

steps.prompt:
He has chewed the aspirin. His own nitroglycerin bottle is in his hand: filled in his name, three months ago, not expired. He rates the pressure an 8 out of 10.

Before you assist with a dose, what must you confirm?

choices.text: Systolic above 100, prescribed to him, not expired, no erectile dysfunction drug in the last 24 to 48 hours, and protocol authorization
choices.feedback: All five, every time. The one providers forget is the PDE-5 question, and patients almost never volunteer it. Ask directly, regardless of the patient's age.

choices.text: Only that the bottle is his and the pressure is above 90
choices.feedback: Missing the expiration check and the PDE-5 question. Sildenafil within 24 hours or tadalafil within 48 hours plus nitroglycerin produces profound hypotension that is very hard to reverse.

choices.text: Nothing, since it is his own prescribed medication
choices.feedback: His prescription does not mean it is safe right now. Blood pressure, expiration and PDE-5 use all change moment to moment, and assisting is still a medication administration you are responsible for.

choices.text: Only that his pain is above a 5 out of 10
choices.feedback: Pain severity is not a criterion for nitroglycerin at all. The criteria are prescription, expiration, blood pressure, PDE-5 exposure and authorization.

steps.prompt: He denies any erectile dysfunction medication, and you confirm this twice. You assist with `0.4 mg` sublingual. Five minutes later he says the pressure has eased to about a 6. You take another blood pressure before considering a second dose.

choices.text: Assist with a second 0.4 mg dose and recheck the pressure again in 5 minutes
choices.feedback: Correct. He is improving, the systolic is comfortably above 100, and he has had one of three permitted doses. Keep checking the pressure before each dose, without exception.

choices.text: Give two doses at once to get ahead of the pain
choices.feedback: Never stack doses. The interval is 5 minutes precisely because the blood pressure response has to be measured between them.

choices.text: Stop nitroglycerin since the pain improved
choices.feedback: Defensible but conservative. He still has active ischemic pain at a 6 and a blood pressure that supports treatment. Continuing within protocol reduces the workload on a starving muscle.

choices.text: Skip further nitroglycerin and transport to the closest hospital, 12 minutes away
choices.feedback: The closest hospital is not the right hospital if it cannot open the artery. And withholding an indicated dose with a systolic of 126 leaves a treatment on the table.

steps.prompt: You are loaded and moving. He has had two doses. He suddenly says he feels lightheaded and looks grayer. You recheck the blood pressure.

choices.text: Withhold the third dose, lay him supine, recheck the pressure, and notify the receiving hospital
choices.feedback: Correct. A systolic of 84 with a falling heart rate is below every threshold. The bradycardia with hypotension raises the question of an inferior and right ventricular infarct, which makes further nitroglycerin dangerous.

choices.text: Give the third dose, since he is still within the three-dose maximum
choices.feedback: The maximum is a ceiling, not a target. Blood pressure is checked before every dose precisely so this dose is not given. A third dose here could drop him into profound hypotension.

choices.text: Sit him fully upright to reduce the workload on his heart
choices.feedback: Sitting a hypotensive patient upright drops cerebral perfusion further. Lay him flat and reassess.

choices.text: Hold nitroglycerin and continue transport without changing anything else
choices.feedback: Holding the dose is right, but a systolic of 84 with a heart rate of 58 deserves a position change, a reassessment and a call ahead. Do not just keep driving.

steps.prompt:
Supine, his pressure comes up to 96/60 and the lightheadedness eases. You are nine minutes from the catheterization center.

What is the most important content of your radio report?

choices.text: 58-year-old with 40 minutes of ischemic chest pain, 12-lead transmitted, aspirin 324 mg given, two doses of nitroglycerin with subsequent hypotension and bradycardia, now supine and improved, ETA nine minutes
choices.feedback: Exactly. The hypotensive response after nitroglycerin with bradycardia is the detail that changes the receiving team's thinking, because it points at right ventricular involvement.

choices.text: Chest pain patient, stable, ETA nine minutes
choices.feedback: Far too thin for a patient whose tracing may already have activated the cath lab. The team needs the medications given and the hypotensive episode.

choices.text: Give the full past medical history and every medication he takes at home
choices.feedback: That detail belongs in the bedside handoff and the written report. The radio report is who, what is wrong, what you did, how he responded, and when you arrive.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: aspirin is nearly always yes, and nitroglycerin is always a decision.

Aspirin `324 mg` chewed, given as four `81 mg` tablets, has the clearest survival benefit of anything in your bag, and the only real reasons to withhold it are a true allergy, active bleeding, or a patient who cannot protect their airway.

Nitroglycerin has five gates every single time: prescribed to this patient, not expired, systolic above `100`, no PDE-5 drug in the last `24-48` hours, and protocol authorization. A blood pressure goes before every dose, not before the first one. That discipline is what caught the drop from `144` to `84` in this case.

The deeper lesson is the bradycardia with hypotension after nitroglycerin. That combination points at an inferior infarct with right ventricular involvement, a ventricle that produces output only when it is full. Nitroglycerin empties it. Lay the patient flat, hold the nitro, and tell the receiving hospital, because it changes what they do next.

And oxygen: only below `94%`, or with dyspnea or shock. Never routinely.

scenarios.title: Witnessed collapse in a gym
scenarios.intro: You are dispatched to a fitness center for a man down. Dispatch reports a 54-year-old collapsed on the gym floor about two minutes ago, bystanders are with him, and an AED is mounted on the wall near the front desk. You and your partner arrive in four minutes with the monitor, airway bag and stretcher.

steps.prompt:
A staff member is kneeling beside a man lying on the rubber floor. She says he was on a treadmill, grabbed his chest, and went down. She has not touched him. He is motionless and gray, and you see occasional irregular gasps. You kneel, tap his shoulder and shout. Nothing.

What do you do in the next ten seconds?

choices.text: Check for a carotid pulse and breathing simultaneously for no more than 10 seconds, and send your partner for the AED
choices.feedback: Correct. Agonal gasps are not breathing. One simultaneous check, ten seconds maximum, while the AED is already on its way. Both things happen at once because you have two people.

choices.text: Begin rescue breaths with a bag-valve mask and reassess in one minute
choices.feedback: This is a witnessed adult collapse during exertion, which is a cardiac arrest until proven otherwise. Ventilation alone wastes the minutes when defibrillation has the highest chance of working.

choices.text: Take a full set of vital signs including a blood pressure
choices.feedback: A blood pressure on an unresponsive, gasping patient tells you nothing you need and costs you a minute you cannot get back.

choices.text: Load him onto the stretcher and begin CPR in the ambulance
choices.feedback: Compressions are worse in a moving vehicle and the delay in moving him costs perfusion. Work the arrest where he lies. The definitive treatment, a shock, is on the wall twenty feet away.

steps.prompt:
No pulse. The gasps are agonal. Your partner is back with the AED in about thirty seconds.

What happens while the pads are being applied?

choices.text: Begin compressions immediately at 100-120 per minute, 2 to 2.4 inches deep, and do not stop while the pads go on
choices.feedback: Correct. Compressions start the instant you confirm no pulse and continue through pad placement. The only pause is the analysis itself.

choices.text: Hold compressions until the pads are attached so the analysis is not disturbed
choices.feedback: Pads are applied during compressions. Every second without compressions drops the pressure in his coronary arteries, and it takes several compressions to build it back.

choices.text: Start compressions but at a slower rate to conserve energy for a long code
choices.feedback: Rate is 100-120 from the first compression. Slower compressions generate less flow, and the fix for fatigue is rotating every two minutes, not compressing badly.

choices.text: Insert an oral airway and ventilate first, then begin compressions
choices.feedback: In a witnessed adult arrest, compressions and defibrillation come first. Airway management follows. Reversed priorities cost survival in a primary cardiac arrest.

steps.prompt:
Pads are on in anterior-lateral position. The AED analyzes and announces shock advised. Everyone is clear and it discharges.

What is your immediate next action?

choices.text: Check for a carotid pulse to see whether it worked
choices.feedback: This is the most common post-shock error. A heart that just converted is not perfusing yet, and the pause lets arterial pressure collapse. Compressions first, pulse check at the next analysis.

choices.text: Resume compressions immediately and continue for 2 minutes before the next analysis
choices.feedback: Correct. No pulse check, no waiting, no discussion. Two full minutes of compressions, with the compressor switching at the next analysis.

choices.text: Wait for the AED to reanalyze before touching the patient
choices.feedback: The AED will not reanalyze for two minutes, and those two minutes are meant to be filled with compressions, not standing still.

choices.text: Give two ventilations, then resume compressions
choices.feedback: Compressions restart immediately after a shock. Ventilations resume in the 30:2 cycle from there, not as a separate step first.

steps.prompt: You complete two minutes at 30 compressions to 2 breaths with an oral airway and bag-valve mask. You switch compressors at the analysis. Shock advised again, delivered, compressions resumed immediately. During the third cycle your partner notes the end-tidal carbon dioxide has jumped from 18 to 44 mmHg.

choices.text: Finish the two-minute cycle, then check for a pulse at the next rhythm analysis
choices.feedback: Correct. A sudden ETCO2 rise strongly suggests ROSC, but you do not interrupt compressions to chase it. Complete the cycle and check at the scheduled pause.

choices.text: Stop compressions immediately and check a pulse
choices.feedback: Tempting, and it is the right suspicion, but an unscheduled interruption costs perfusion. The check happens at the next analysis, which is seconds away.

choices.text: Ignore it, since end-tidal carbon dioxide is not useful during CPR
choices.feedback: The opposite is true. ETCO2 reflects pulmonary blood flow, so it measures compression quality and is often the first sign of ROSC, before any pulse is palpable.

choices.text: Increase the ventilation rate to take advantage of the returning circulation
choices.feedback: Hyperventilation raises pressure in the chest and reduces venous return, which is exactly what a barely returning circulation cannot tolerate.

steps.prompt: At the analysis the AED advises no shock. You check the carotid and feel a strong, regular pulse. He is not breathing on his own. Your partner has the bag ready.

choices.text: Ventilate at 1 breath every 6 seconds, titrate oxygen toward 94-98%, leave the pads on, and obtain a 12-lead
choices.feedback: Correct on every count. Ten breaths a minute, not more. Pads stay on because re-arrest is common, and the 12-lead may change the destination.

choices.text: Ventilate at 20 breaths per minute to make up for the arrest
choices.feedback: The classic post-ROSC error. Hyperventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, cuts venous return and constricts cerebral vessels in a brain that just survived an arrest.

choices.text: Remove the pads so they do not interfere with the 12-lead
choices.feedback: Leave them on. Re-arrest in the first minutes is common and you want to shock without setting up again. The pads do not prevent a 12-lead.

choices.text: Stop ventilating and apply a nonrebreather at 15 L/min
choices.feedback: He is not breathing on his own. A mask delivers nothing to a patient with no respiratory effort. Continue positive pressure ventilation at 10 per minute.

steps.prompt:
He is ventilated, saturating at 96%, with a pulse of 100 and a systolic in the 90s. The 12-lead shows an infarct pattern. The nearest hospital is eight minutes away and has no catheterization lab. A cardiac center is nineteen minutes away.

Where do you go?

choices.text: The cardiac center, notifying them early, because opening the artery is the definitive treatment and he is being effectively supported
choices.feedback: Correct where protocol allows it. A post-arrest patient with an infarct pattern needs a catheterization lab, and the extra eleven minutes buys definitive care.

choices.text: The nearest hospital, because any hospital is better than a longer transport
choices.feedback: Defensible if he becomes unstable or you cannot ventilate him, and some systems mandate it. But a stable, supported post-arrest infarct patient benefits from the specialty center.

choices.text: Stay on scene to stabilize him further before choosing
choices.feedback: There is nothing left to do on scene. Definitive care is a catheterization lab, and delaying transport only increases the chance he re-arrests where you have fewer resources.

scenarios.debrief:
The pattern: in a witnessed adult collapse, compressions and defibrillation outrank everything else, and interruptions are what kill.

The numbers this case tested: rate `100-120`, depth `2 to 2.4 inches` in an adult, `30:2` without an advanced airway, compressor switch every `2 minutes` timed to the analysis, interruptions under `10 seconds`, and compression fraction above `60%`.

The single most-failed step is the one right after a shock. There is no pulse check. Compressions resume immediately and run a full two minutes, because a heart that just converted is not yet perfusing and the pause drops the pressure you spent minutes building.

End-tidal carbon dioxide is your quality meter and your earliest ROSC signal. A sudden jump above about `40 mmHg` usually precedes a palpable pulse, but it does not earn an unscheduled interruption.

And after ROSC: `1 breath every 6 seconds`, oxygen titrated to `94-98%`, pads left on, a `12-lead`, and a destination that can open the artery. The most common post-ROSC error in real life is bagging too fast because the room is excited. Count out loud.
